title: Commutant of a Cyclic Matrix is K[M]
description: Proves the third classical characterization of nonderogatory matrices: if M has a cyclic vector, then every matrix commuting with M is a polynomial in M. Equivalently, the centralizer of M coincides with the algebra K[M] and is commutative. A structural consequence of the cyclic-vector theorem (Hoffman & Kunze §7.5), over an arbitrary field. 0 sorries, 0 axioms (machine-verified).

meta.author: Lean Genius Research
meta.assumptions: No axioms or sorries. Machine-verified under Docker (full build, 7745 jobs). Uses only Mathlib's Polynomial, Matrix, and Module.Basis APIs (Mathlib v4.26.0).
originalContributions: commuting_matrix_is_polynomial: if M has a cyclic vector v and A*M = M*A, then A = aeval M p for some polynomial p — the centralizer of M is contained in K[M]
commutant_commutative: any two matrices commuting with a cyclic matrix M commute with each other (the centralizer is commutative)
aeval_commute: every polynomial in M commutes with M — the trivial inclusion K[M] ⊆ centralizer(M), which together with commuting_matrix_is_polynomial gives centralizer(M) = K[M]
krylov_linearIndependent: the Krylov vectors {Mᵏ·v} of a cyclic vector are linearly independent, hence a basis of Kⁿ
meta.historicalContext: A matrix is nonderogatory when its minimal polynomial equals its characteristic polynomial. Three classical conditions are equivalent (Hoffman & Kunze, 'Linear Algebra', §7.2 and §7.5): (i) minpoly = charpoly; (ii) M has a cyclic vector; (iii) the only matrices commuting with M are the polynomials in M. The parent entries settle (i)⟺(ii) over arbitrary fields. This entry proves the (ii)⟹(iii) direction — that a cyclic vector forces the centralizer to collapse to K[M] — completing the bridge to the third characterization. The result is the linear-algebra core of the statement that a nonderogatory matrix's centralizer has dimension exactly n.
meta.proofStrategy: The Krylov vectors {v, Mv, …, M^{n-1}v} of the cyclic vector form a basis of Kⁿ. Given A commuting with M, expand A·v in this basis to obtain a polynomial p with p(M)·v = A·v. Because A and p(M) both commute with every power Mⁱ, they agree on every basis vector Mⁱ·v, hence on all of Kⁿ; a matrix is determined by its action, so A = p(M).

overview.problemStatement:
**Open question from cayley-hamilton-cyclic-vector-all-fields**: The parent biconditional shows a matrix $M \in K^{n\times n}$ is nonderogatory iff it has a cyclic vector. The textbook characterization has a third equivalent condition: the centralizer of $M$ equals the polynomial algebra $K[M]$. Does a cyclic vector force every commuting matrix to be a polynomial in $M$?

Formally: if $v$ is cyclic for $M$ and $AM = MA$, must there exist $p \in K[X]$ with $A = p(M)$?
overview.historicalContext: For $M \in K^{n\times n}$, the **centralizer** (or commutant) is $C(M) = \{A : AM = MA\}$. Always $K[M] \subseteq C(M)$. The reverse inclusion characterizes nonderogatory matrices: $C(M) = K[M]$ iff $\dim_K C(M) = n$ iff $M$ is nonderogatory iff $M$ has a cyclic vector (Hoffman–Kunze §7.5). The cyclic-vector hypothesis is exactly what makes the evaluation map $p \mapsto p(M)\cdot v$ surjective onto $K^n$, which pins any commuting $A$ down to a single polynomial determined by where it sends $v$. This is the structural fact behind, e.g., the description of matrices commuting with a companion matrix.
keyInsights: The Krylov vectors {v, Mv, …, M^{n-1}v} of a cyclic vector are linearly independent (the converse of the cyclic condition), hence form a basis of Kⁿ since there are exactly n of them.
A commuting matrix A is fully determined by the single image A·v: expanding A·v in the Krylov basis yields coordinates cₖ, and p := ∑ cₖ Xᵏ satisfies p(M)·v = A·v.
A and p(M) agree on the whole Krylov basis: A·(Mⁱv) = Mⁱ·(A·v) = Mⁱ·(p(M)·v) = p(M)·(Mⁱv), using that both A and p(M) commute with every power of M.
Agreement on a basis upgrades to A·w = p(M)·w for all w (linearity of mulVec), and a matrix is recovered column-by-column from its action on standard basis vectors, giving A = p(M).
Commutativity of the centralizer follows immediately: if A and B both commute with M they are both polynomials in M, and polynomials in M commute with each other since K[X] is commutative.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Step 1**: `krylov_linearIndependent` — from `IsCyclicVector M v`, the family `k ↦ Mᵏ·v` is linearly independent (build a degree-`<n` polynomial from any vanishing relation and apply the cyclic hypothesis). With `basisOfLinearIndependentOfCardEqFinrank` and `Module.finrank_fintype_fun_eq_card`, this becomes a basis `b` of `Fin n → K`.

**Step 2**: Set `p := ∑ₖ C(b.repr (A·v) k) · Xᵏ`. Then `p(M)·v = ∑ₖ (coords) • (Mᵏ·v) = ∑ₖ (coords) • b k = A·v` by `Basis.sum_repr`.

**Step 3**: For each `i`, `A·(b i) = p(M)·(b i)` via `Matrix.mulVec_mulVec` and the two commutation facts (`Commute.pow_right` for A, `aeval_commute_pow` for p(M)).

**Step 4**: Linearity (`Matrix.mulVecLin`, `map_sum`, `map_smul`) lifts agreement-on-basis to `∀ w, A·w = p(M)·w`; column extraction (`Pi.single`, `dotProduct`) gives `A = p(M)`.

openQuestions: Does the centralizer-equals-K[M] characterization admit a clean dimension statement in Lean — that dim_K C(M) = n exactly when M is nonderogatory — building on the inclusion proved here?
Conversely, if the centralizer of M equals K[M], does M necessarily have a cyclic vector? This is the (iii)⟹(ii) direction completing the triple equivalence.

How does the commutant behave for derogatory matrices: the centralizer strictly contains K[M], and its dimension equals ∑ (2i−1) dᵢ over the invariant-factor degrees dᵢ (Frobenius). Formalizing this dimension formula would generalize the result here.

sections.title: Main theorem: commuting_matrix_is_polynomial
sections.summary: If M has a cyclic vector v and A*M = M*A then A = aeval M p for some p. Builds the Krylov basis, defines p from the coordinates of A·v, shows A and p(M) agree on the basis using both commutation facts, lifts to all vectors by linearity, and recovers A = p(M) column-by-column.

sections.title: Consequences: commutant_commutative and aeval_commute
sections.summary: The centralizer of a cyclic matrix is commutative (any two commuting matrices are polynomials in M, which commute), and the trivial inclusion K[M] ⊆ centralizer(M) — together giving centralizer(M) = K[M].

conclusion.summary: A cyclic vector forces the centralizer of M to be exactly the polynomial algebra K[M]: every matrix commuting with M is a polynomial in M, and the centralizer is therefore commutative. This is the third classical characterization of nonderogatory matrices, formalized over an arbitrary field as a structural consequence of the cyclic-vector theorem.
conclusion.implications: Together with the parent biconditional (nonderogatory ⟺ cyclic vector), this entry supplies the (ii)⟹(iii) edge of the standard triple equivalence (minpoly = charpoly ⟺ cyclic vector ⟺ centralizer = K[M]). It is the linear-algebra core of the statement that a nonderogatory matrix has an n-dimensional, commutative centralizer, and underlies the description of matrices commuting with a companion matrix.
openQuestions: Prove the converse edge (iii)⟹(ii): if the centralizer of M equals K[M], then M has a cyclic vector, closing the triple equivalence.
Formalize the dimension statement dim_K C(M) = n for nonderogatory M, and the Frobenius formula for the derogatory case.
Lift the result to the endomorphism setting (Module.End) rather than concrete matrices, for reuse across the gallery's linear-algebra entries.
